senses: Brash, self-promoting.
Of or like figs.
Containing figs.
ety: From fig + -y. However, figgy pudding has a different origin; see Figgy pudding#Etymology on Wikipedia.

senses: A handbell used for summoning monks.
The "bell" or flaring mouth of a trumpet.
ety: From Latin codon, from Ancient Greek κώδων (kṓdōn).

senses: An academic discipline that attempts to understand the social orders people use to make sense of the world through analysing their accounts and descriptions of their day-to-day experiences.
A mixture of bark, dried leaves, and often berries and/or tobacco, which is smoked.
ety: Originally spelled with an "l" in the first part (i.e. killikinick, killikinnick). From Unami këlëkënikàn (“smoking mixture, killikinick”).

senses: A standard-bearer.
A rank of noble introduced by King Cnut
A type of shag tobacco.
examples: She had been sitting there for nearly an hour and a half, and during that time she had drunk two glasses of black coffee, smoked six caporal cigarettes and read the week's Candide.

senses: A pintail duck, a type of dabbling duck with a characteristic pointed tail.
A northern pintail, Anas acuta, a dabbling duck of the northern hemisphere that has a long pointed tail.
A pin-tailed snipe, Gallinago stenura.
Bearing resemblance to an ape or monkey; apelike or monkeylike.
ety: From Latin sīmia (“ape, monkey”), from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”).

senses: A crustless quiche: a molded omelette in which vegetables, cheese, etc., are mixed into the eggs and cooked together.
ety: Borrowed from Italian frittata, from fritto (“fried”).

senses: A shelf set into a mineshaft for storing waste material, or for use as a step or support.
ety: Borrowed from Low German Stempel or Dutch stempel, akin to Old English stempan (“to stamp”), all from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną (“to compress, squeeze, stamp”).

senses: Having multiple nuclei; multinucleate
Resin derived from this tree, once sometimes used in the production of rubber.
Resembling the sound of a rattle.
Of a vehicle, that shakes when being driven.
Of the lungs, chest, etc., producing raspy or gurgling sound due to excess mucus.
A driver of an automobile, especially a getaway vehicle in a criminal enterprise.
examples: For instance, the wheelman in a robbery; he doesn't intend for anyone to get killed when he pulls up in front of a liquor store so that his armed complice can rob the store.

senses: elder brother
friend, dude, man
ety: Borrowed from Hindi भैया (bhaiyā). Sense 3 originates from the common usage of this word among Hindi speakers who migrate into parts of India where Hindi is not commonly spoken.

senses: Either of two folded sheets of paper used to connect the front and back covers of a book to the first and last pages; one side of each endpaper is glued to the cover board, and the other side forms a flyleaf.
Any upright or console model phonograph from the early 1900s, usually with a wooden cabinet body and an interior horn for the projection of sound, that plays 78 rpm records using a steel needle.
Any device that maintains or applies tension
A small photographic developing and printing system.
examples: Some of those kiosks are free-standing, and others are connected to an in-store minilab.

senses: Having a tinkling sound.
examples: The tinkly piano-playing soon got on my nerves.

senses: To join or link together, as though in a chain.
ety: From the perfect passive participle stem of Latin concatēnāre (“to link or chain together”), from con- (“with”) + catēnō (“chain, bind”), from catēna (“a chain”).

senses: An investigative reporter.
examples: I recently received a firsthand report from an old friend — John A. Keel — who until last year was as skeptical a newshound as I have known.

senses: A paste made from ground sesame seeds, and used to make hummus, baba ganoush, etc.
ety: From Arabic طَحِينَة (ṭaḥīna), from the root ط ح ن (ṭ-ḥ-n) related to grinding. Final -i most probably from North Levantine dialects or from Greek ταχίνι (tachíni).

senses: To become happier.
To make happier.
To make the sound of a bird; to chirp.
ety: From Middle English chirken, cherken, charken, from Old English ċearcian (“to chatter, creak, crash”), from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn (“to make a sound, crack”). Doublet of chark. Related also to crake, crack.

senses: A jug for holding cream.
A separator for removing cream from milk to leave skimmed milk.
A nondairy product that adds a creamy texture to coffee.
To treat or anoint with balsam.
ety: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon, “balsam”), of Semitic origin (Hebrew בושם (“spice, perfume”)); compare Old English balsam, balsamum (“balsam, balm”), Doublet of balm and desman. Not related to balsa.

senses: A particular variety of Cucurbita pepo, a small marrow/squash.
The edible fruit of this marrow/squash.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French courgette, diminutive of courge (“vegetable marrow, marrow squash”). Ultimately related to zucchini through Latin cucurbita.

senses: To make (more) dense.
To become (more) dense.
examples: Some space missions cool the propellant to almost freezing to densify it, so they can fit more fuel and oxidizer in the tanks.

senses: as measured using a bolometer
To keep or put (something, especially a liquid) in, or as if in, a phial.
ety: The noun is derived partly: * from Middle English fiole, phiole, phial (“small bowl or cup for liquids, etc.; flask”) [and other forms], from Middle French fiole, phiole [and other forms], and Old French fiole (modern French fiole), from Late Latin fiola, phiola, from Latin phiala (“broad, flat, shallow bowl or cup”), from Ancient Greek φιάλη (phiálē, “round and shallow bowl, pan, or saucer”), probably from Pre-Greek; and * directly from Latin phiala (see above). senses: A person who makes a claim; a claimant.
A pretender to a royal title.
A racehorse offered for sale before a race and delivered to the buyer afterwards.
A claiming race.
examples: He did not have a proper claiming authorization on file, and contended that the trainer had not asked his permission to enter the horse in a claimer.

senses: Causing irritation or inflammation.
ety: From French irritant, equivalent to irritate + -ant.

senses: One who engages in sexual acts with corpses.
An uncultivated plain, especially a sandy track along the seashore in southwestern France.
ety: Borrowed from French lande, from Middle French lande, from Old French lande (“clearing in a wood, leigh; remote wooded area”). Doublet of lawn and land.

senses: Thriving under acidic conditions; relating to or being an acidophile.
Easily stained with acidic dyes, such as eosin.
A small electrical appliance for drying hair, by generating a stream of hot air.
Of or like glass, especially in being smooth and somewhat reflective.
Including a lot of glass.
Extensively glazed.
Dull; expressionless; lifeless.
ety: From Middle English glasy, equivalent to glass + -y. Compare Saterland Frisian glääsich (“glassy”), Dutch glazig (“glassy”), German Low German glasig (“glassy”), German glasig (“glassy”).

senses: A South American mammal of the camel family, Lama glama, used as a domestic beast of burden and a source of wool and meat.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish llama, from Quechua llama.

senses: Espousing a unitary view of God.
Espousing a unitary view of national government.
